# Game Design at the Edge of 2026: From MDA to Adaptive, AI-Mediated, and Participatory Systems

As of September 2026, the most consequential advances in game design are not a single replacement for established theory but a change in what a game is designed to do. Game systems are increasingly adaptive, generated or co-created with AI, embodied through XR and haptics, and extended by player communities. The strongest evidence supports faster exploration, richer personalization, stronger embodiment, and more accessible participation in particular prototypes and contexts; it does not yet support universal claims that AI, biometric adaptation, or any newer framework reliably produces better games.

MDA remains valuable because it gives teams a compact language for tracing mechanics into runtime dynamics and player experience. Its weaknesses—especially its loose ontology, limited treatment of interfaces and context, and lack of a predictive formula—have motivated RMDA, DDE, DPE, IP-MDA, experience-driven adaptation, procedural-rhetoric, Values at Play, and co-creative AI approaches. Yet the supplied evidence contains no direct head-to-head study showing that any extension consistently outperforms MDA across genres, cultures, or player populations.

The practical conclusion is therefore twofold: retain MDA as a shared system-to-experience vocabulary, but supplement it with explicit models of interface feedback, player agency, values, adaptation, community governance, production constraints, and commercial incentives.

## How the report resolves the main questions

The report first maps the major 2024–2026 developments and separates scholarly findings from official engine documentation, product announcements, and industry reports. It then reconstructs MDA, examines its extensions and applications, and compares it with newer approaches on shared axes: causal direction, abstraction level, experience modeling, adaptation, values, IP, and designer control.

The middle sections treat cutting-edge theories as design arguments rather than fashionable labels. For each, they identify the central claim, the design phenomenon it addresses, the evidence supporting it, its limitations, and its practical implication. Contemporary cases—including *Split Fiction*, *Journey*, *Code: Terror*, Roblox creator ecosystems, *Poder Violeta 2*, and AI-generated prototypes—show how those theories become mechanics, dynamics, experiences, workflows, and evaluation criteria.

The final sections synthesize benefits and risks. They distinguish what current evidence demonstrates from what remains a product promise or a research proposal, then identify the most important unresolved questions: direct framework comparisons, controlled human–AI studies, longitudinal adaptive systems, cross-platform UGC governance, privacy-preserving sensing, and standardized measures of game feel, originality, player welfare, and community health.

## 1. The current state of game design and recent developments

### A field moving from authored artifacts to responsive systems

A broad scoping review by Berger mapped game-design research into ten categories containing 78 independent or interdependent aspects, including design aims, design process, gameplay, representation, character design, social interaction, narratology, game analysis, serious games, and gamification. The review was intentionally exploratory: it included non-peer-reviewed and unpublished material and did not assess evidence quality, so it is useful as a map of the field rather than as a ranking of validated methods. [Berger’s scoping review](https://repositum.tuwien.at/bitstream/20.500.12708/20359/1/Berger%20Lukas%20-%202022%20-%20Key%20aspects%20of%20game%20design%20-%20a%20scoping%20review.pdf)

Recent work adds a new organizing principle to that map. The important question is no longer only “What mechanics should be authored?” but also:

- What can be generated or recombined?
- What can be inferred about the player?
- What should adapt at runtime?
- Who is allowed to create?
- Which values and risks are built into the system?
- How can the resulting experience be evaluated?

A systematic review of 74 studies published from 2020 through April 2025 found AI embedded across all stages of game design, including collaborative development, personalized content adaptation, dynamic difficulty adjustment, affective computing, and generative technologies. The same review identified technology-integration complexity and insufficient interdisciplinary validation as persistent limitations, recommending standardized evaluation frameworks. [Systematic review of AI-driven game design and UX research](https://doi.org/10.30560/hssr.v8n4p229)

A separate scoping review of 177 GPT-for-games papers, 122 of them published in 2024, identified five major application areas: procedural content generation, mixed-initiative game design, mixed-initiative gameplay, game-playing agents, and game-user research. Its central implication is that the important design problem is not generation alone but interaction between models and users. [GPT for Games: An Updated Scoping Review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00308)

The research landscape therefore points toward a shift from a mostly one-way pipeline—designer authors rules, player encounters them—to a set of feedback loops:

1. A designer or player specifies an intention.
2. A tool generates, proposes, or modifies content.
3. The engine validates or executes it.
4. Players interact with the result.
5. Telemetry, physiological data, social behavior, or qualitative feedback are interpreted.
6. The system or team changes the next version of the content.

That loop can improve iteration, but it also makes design responsibility harder to locate. A designer may no longer specify every encounter, yet still remains responsible for the constraints, incentives, data collection, moderation, and failure modes that shape what the system produces.

### The main recent developments

| Advancement | Date and evidence type | Design impact | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generative and mixed-initiative AI | 2024–2026 scholarly reviews, professional surveys, prototypes, and official engine documentation | Faster ideation, asset exploration, code assistance, procedural variation, and model-assisted testing | Independent measures of productivity, originality, quality, and player experience remain sparse |
| Experience-driven and emotion-sensitive adaptation | 2025 systematic review; small controlled DDA and physiological studies; 2026 conceptual models | Difficulty and content can respond to performance, engagement, stress, or inferred emotion | Models are often small-sample, opaque, noisy, short-term, or not actually closed-loop |
| XR, haptics, and embodied interaction | 2024 HaptX experiment; 2025 haptic tools and XR heuristics; 2026 emotion-sensing work | Stronger embodiment, object perception, social presence, and alternative access modes | Hardware cost, movement restrictions, calibration, privacy, and limited laboratory samples |
| UGC and creator-platform design | 2025–2026 systematic UGC surveys, child-player and creator studies, official platform releases, industry reports | Creation becomes part of play; communities extend content, retention, monetization, and cultural expression | Access, moderation, discovery, creator precarity, and long-term community effects remain under-researched |
| Values-sensitive, critical, and inclusive design | 2024–2026 participatory and governance studies, Values at Play applications, accessibility guidance | Designers can make representation, safety, agency, and accessibility explicit design objectives | Intent does not establish behavior change; guidance often lacks standardized outcome measures |
| Live-service experimentation and monetization design | 2024 analytical modeling, 2025 netnography, 2026 case analysis and platform tooling | Difficulty curves, prices, matchmaking, retention, and social health become continuously tunable | Engagement metrics may reward pressure, FOMO, opaque adaptation, or harmful economic incentives |

The table combines unlike evidence types. A controlled experiment can estimate a narrow player outcome; a qualitative study can reveal a mechanism or lived experience; official documentation can establish that a tool exists; and an industry report can describe scale or market direction. None automatically substitutes for another.

### Generative AI: adoption is real, validation is not

A mixed-method study of game-design professionals surveyed 42 participants and interviewed 9. In that exploratory sample, 90.5% reported using generative AI for ideation and brainstorming, 83.3% for asset creation, and 73.8% for programming. Participants also described faster ideation, enhanced prototyping, and automation of repetitive work, alongside concerns about originality, creative dependency, and the weakening of human-authored content. The study recruited through a professional and semi-professional developer community, so its percentages should not be treated as industry-wide estimates. [Generative AI in Game Design](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12193870/)

A 2026 CHI synthesis reached a related but more cautious conclusion. It used interpretive meta-ethnography to synthesize ten eligible qualitative studies from literature published between 2020 and 2025. The synthesis reports that at least 7% of games released on Steam disclosed some AI use for content creation, compared with 1% the previous year, and that roughly 60% of disclosed implementations involved visual assets. These are disclosure-based Steam figures, not a census of AI use, and they say nothing by themselves about whether the resulting games are better. [Generative AI in Game Development](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791206)

The practical pattern is mixed initiative rather than autonomous substitution. AI is most reliable when the designer can inspect, reject, constrain, and revise outputs. It is less reliable when the intended design depends on hidden context, engine-specific conventions, long-range systemic consistency, or nuanced game feel.

### Adaptive experience: from difficulty curves to control loops

The 2025 systematic review *Closing the Loop* analyzed 17 empirical studies of complete experience-driven adaptation systems. Its architecture has three components: player-driven data, a player-experience model, and content adaptation. Telemetry was the most common sensing modality, while facial-expression analysis and peripheral interaction data were underused. Knowledge-based rules and heuristics dominated because they were interpretable and inexpensive; machine-learning approaches promised greater personalization but faced data-availability and transparency problems. [Closing the Loop](https://arxiv.org/html/2505.01351v1)

Difficulty remained the most common adaptation objective. Stress, anxiety, and other affective states were largely neglected, even though they matter in immersive, therapeutic, and mental-health applications. The design problem is consequently not simply “make the game harder or easier,” but “decide which player state matters, how confidently it can be inferred, and what intervention will produce the intended next state.”

The results are conditional. A 2025 EDDA study tested 100 participants aged 19–29 across seven genres over six weeks. Gameplay time and Game Engagement Questionnaire scores differed significantly across baseline, simplified, and full EDDA conditions, but the overall fitness measure did not show a significant difference. The authors nevertheless report positive post-hoc intervention evidence, making the fitness conclusion mixed rather than definitive. The study’s age range, genre distribution, duration, and prototype design limit generalization. [Applied Sciences EDDA study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/10/5610)

Other studies demonstrate why adaptation must be parameterized carefully. A 2025 physiological-DDA study used a hybrid LSTM to predict challenge and engagement from multimodal signals in 10 participants and evaluated the approach with 12 participants. Physiological DDA increased engagement relative to single-level and gradually increasing difficulty, and increased cognitive challenge without increasing workload, but the samples were small. [Physiological DDA study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3714394.3756169)

A 2025 review of biofeedback DDA describes *Code: Terror*, a Unity 6 survival-horror prototype using smartwatch heart rate, voice level, and heart-rate variability. In a 40-person experiment, the DDA condition produced higher IMI and CORGIS scores and lower heart-rate ranges. However, the same review describes a different heart-rate game, *Caroline*, in which biofeedback DDA improved intrinsic motivation but did not significantly affect decision-making difficulty, cognitive difficulty, emotional challenge, or performance. A VR study using EMG and heart rate to adapt enemy frequency and damage increased physical challenge and frustration. [Electronics review of biofeedback DDA](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/19/3870)

These results do not contradict one another. They show that adaptation is an intervention, not a guaranteed benefit. The same stress estimate can support calmness, intensify challenge, or create unfairness depending on the parameter changed, the player’s interpretation, and the timing of the change.

### XR and haptics: embodiment as a design variable

A 2024 HaptX study with 32 participants found that kinesthetic gloves strengthened the embodiment illusion during full-body avatar control in immersive VR. The gloves also supplied useful cues about basic three-dimensional structure and stiffness in an object-discrimination task. The study used a laboratory prototype with an HTC VIVE headset, HaptX DK2 gloves, trackers, Unity, SteamVR, and the HaptX SDK. Participants were drawn from a local university community, and the cable between the gloves and backpack restricted free-limb movement to a 1.5-by-1.5-meter area. [Frontiers in Virtual Reality study](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/virtual-reality/articles/10.3389/frvir.2024.1439724/full)

The design implication is not that every game needs force-feedback gloves. It is that embodiment can be designed through correspondence between action, sensation, and world consequence. A haptic signal can communicate an object’s stiffness, an avatar’s bodily state, a weapon’s resistance, or another player’s presence. But the signal must be authored as part of the game’s feedback grammar, not appended as generic vibration.

Tooling is moving in that direction. A 2025 Unity plugin provides reusable haptic assets, graphical curve editing, more than 40 curve presets, scripting, audio conversion, and an AI Haptic Advisor using GPT-3.5 and DeepSeek R1 APIs. The source reports workflow functionality, not a controlled comparison of player outcomes. It also identifies persistent barriers: specialized hardware is expensive, programming requires expertise, and industry standards remain weak. [Applied Sciences haptic authoring study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/10/5419)

A 2025 XR UX study formalized 13 heuristic principles from 13 scholarly articles, applied them to seven XR games, and trained a retrieval-augmented-generation model on 1,515 case instances. The principles improved agreement between gamers and HCI researchers about terminology and categories, while the AI model provided a baseline for mapping accuracy and efficiency. The supplied record gives no numerical accuracy or effect size, so the result supports standardization more strongly than it supports automated evaluation. [XR UX heuristic study](https://doi.org/10.46248/kidrs.2025.3.215)

### UGC: creation, economy, and governance become game design

UGC is no longer merely an optional level editor. On large platforms, it is simultaneously a content pipeline, a social system, a monetization architecture, a moderation problem, and a player-retention strategy.

A 2025 taxonomy-driven survey replaced a rigid classification of UGC with two non-exclusive dimensions: gameplay and resource files. Gameplay includes game modes that change core mechanics and levels or campaigns that retain the base mechanics while adding challenges. Resource changes include new instruments, objects, and global impacts. The taxonomy is useful because many contemporary creations are hybrids rather than cleanly separable mods. [ACM survey of UGC and game editors](https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3798165)

The same survey found that most research remained confined to one platform or genre, with little comparative or longitudinal analysis of retention, community norms, commercial strategies, creator access, or user judgments of quality. AI-assisted editors such as LSTM-based *Super Mario Bros.* generation, gameplay-video-based level generation, and World-GAN for Minecraft demonstrate technical possibility, but many such tools remain aimed at professional level designers rather than ordinary players.

An industry report from Naavik estimates that developers across Roblox, Fortnite, and Overwolf received approximately $2.2 billion in payouts in 2025, up 47% from 2024. This is a market estimate covering three ecosystems, not a complete measure of all UGC. The report also describes Roblox’s growth, live-operations tooling, creator analytics, custom matchmaking, and a safety analytics dashboard. These developments show the professionalization of UGC, but the report documents platform scale and capability rather than controlled evidence that a particular tool improves player welfare or design quality. [Naavik’s State of UGC Games 2026](https://naavik.co/deep-dives/the-state-of-ugc-games-2026/)

Governance is part of the design system. A CHI PLAY study of Roblox creator discussions identified three ways co-ideation can become risky: directly generating harmful ideas, navigating policy boundaries while developing them, and sharing strategies for bypassing moderation. A separate study of 26 U.S. child players who had used Roblox, Minecraft, Rec Room, or Fortnite Creative identified scams, normalized antisocial behavior, and adult roleplay as three categories of risk. The child-player study also found that automatic detection struggles with evolving risks and that age restrictions can be bypassed or raise privacy concerns. [Zhang and colleagues on harmful design ideation](https://doi.org/10.1145/3677076) · [Child-player study of UGG safety](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3713043.3728858)

The design lesson is consequential: a system that lowers the cost of creation also lowers the cost of producing harmful, manipulative, or low-quality experiences. Safety cannot be treated as a post-publication filter alone. Constraints, reporting tools, creator education, discovery incentives, economic rules, and appeals processes all shape the dynamics of the creator ecosystem.

### Accessibility and inclusive design are becoming production criteria

Microsoft’s Xbox Accessibility Guidelines organize guidance across text, visual and audio cues, captions, screen narration, input, difficulty, object clarity, haptics, time limits, motion, communication, documentation, and mental-health practices. Microsoft describes them as idea generators for designers, guardrails for developers, and a validation checklist for test teams, explicitly stating that they are not a legal-compliance checklist. [Xbox Accessibility Guidelines](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/xbox/accessibility/guidelines)

The distinction matters. Accessibility guidance can change mechanics and dynamics, not merely presentation. A time limit may need to be adjustable; a visual-only warning may need an audio or haptic equivalent; a cooperative task may need to support different action speeds; a menu may need to minimize fatigue.

GameIN in Portugal used 30 monthly co-design sessions with 28 neurodivergent adults aged 19–54. The resulting kit included three games across digital, tabletop, and physical platforms and two adapted tabletop games. Its design criterion was shared play regardless of individual skills and specificities. The source reports successful integration of participant perspectives but no standardized accessibility or engagement effect. [GameIN action research project](https://papers.academic-conferences.org/index.php/ecgbl/article/view/4031)

This evidence supports inclusion as a design process and a shared-play objective. It does not establish that participatory design automatically produces better outcomes for every population.

## 2. MDA: foundations, recent research, and extensions

### What MDA actually says

Hunicke, LeBlanc, and Zubek developed MDA through a Game Design and Tuning Workshop held at the Game Developers Conference between 2001 and 2004. They presented it as a formal approach connecting game design and development, game criticism, and technical game research. [The original MDA paper](https://users.cs.northwestern.edu/~hunicke/MDA.pdf)

| Layer | Definition | Designer’s concern | Player-facing question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanics | Components at the level of data representation, algorithms, and rules | What actions, resources, constraints, and responses are available? | What can I do, and what does the system permit? |
| Dynamics | Runtime behavior produced by mechanics acting on player inputs and one another over time | What patterns of play will emerge? | What is happening as I act and react? |
| Aesthetics | Desirable emotional responses evoked when the player interacts with the system | What experience should the system support? | What do I feel, value, notice, or seek? |

The model has two useful directions. From the designer’s perspective, mechanics are authored to produce dynamics that support aesthetics. From the player’s perspective, the experienced aesthetic and dynamics reveal the underlying mechanics. The reversal is important because a designer may intend one relationship while the player experiences another.

MDA’s aesthetic vocabulary avoids treating every desired outcome as “fun.” Its eight categories are sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression, and submission. A competitive game may prioritize challenge; a social game may prioritize fellowship; a sandbox may prioritize expression and discovery; a low-commitment game may prioritize submission or pastime.

The framework’s restraint is one of its strengths. The original paper explicitly says there is no Grand Unified Theory or formula specifying the combination and proportion of elements that will produce fun. MDA is a vocabulary and tuning lens, not a fun-producing algorithm.

### Why the framework remains useful

MDA makes causal reasoning visible. Consider a basic design question: players in a competitive board game become so wealthy early that later turns no longer feel consequential. The MDA analysis identifies the mechanics that generate income, the dynamics of widening advantage, and the aesthetic consequence: reduced tension, agency, and competition. Possible interventions include subsidies for lagging players, taxes on leading players, time pressure, or resource depletion. Each intervention can then be playtested for secondary effects.

The original Monopoly example also demonstrates an important caveat: a mathematically elegant balancing rule can harm experience if players cannot track it. Complex taxes may technically improve the wealth distribution while making cash, progress, and standings harder to understand. In MDA terms, a mechanic intended to repair a dynamic may damage the player’s sense of investment and feedback.

The framework is also valuable for target-specific design. The MDA paper’s “AI Babysitter” illustration changes the intended aesthetics and audience across a game for children aged 3–7, a *Rugrats*-style game for girls aged 7–12, and a military stealth simulation for men aged 14–35. The resulting changes are not cosmetic. They require different navigation, reasoning, enemy behavior, equipment, skill trees, time pressure, and emotional monitoring. A change in aesthetic target can therefore require a new mechanical and systemic foundation.

### What MDA leaves unresolved

MDA’s first limitation is ontological. Junior and Silva argue that game design lacks a widely accepted ontology and fixed vocabulary, with “mechanics” serving as a recurring example of definitional conflict. They note that the Game Ontology Project’s last entry was in 2015 and that *The 400 Rules of Game Design* listed only 112 of its intended 400 rules before activity stopped. [Redefining the MDA Framework](https://www.mdpi.com/2078-2489/12/10/395)

The second limitation is scope. MDA’s original layers do not explicitly distinguish narrative, interface, audiovisual feedback, accessibility, community governance, commercial incentives, or the social and cultural context in which play occurs. These elements still affect aesthetics, but a team using only MDA may have no shared place to document them.

The third limitation is prediction. Dynamics emerge from player input and system interaction, so they cannot all be known in advance. The more complex the game, the less credible it is to treat the mechanics-to-dynamics relation as deterministic. A designer can predict important dynamics, but playtesting remains essential for discovering unanticipated loops, exploits, social norms, and interpretations.

The fourth limitation is production. MDA tells a team what kind of relationship to examine, but not always how to translate an aesthetic objective into a production schedule, interface specification, narrative structure, learning outcome, moderation policy, or telemetry model.

These limits do not make MDA obsolete. They define the conditions under which it should be supplemented.

### Recent applications of MDA

A computational-thinking educational game integrated MDA into the design phase of ADDIE and the pre-production phase of a Game Development Life Cycle. Subject experts rated it 81%, media experts 91.25%, and user testing produced a 79.8% result. These figures support the feasibility and perceived suitability of the particular prototype; they are not evidence that MDA itself caused the scores or that the results generalize to educational games broadly. [Computational-thinking game study](https://doi.org/10.35959/jik.v13i02.718)

A webtoon-IP study turned MDA into a four-stage iterative workflow:

1. Set an aesthetic goal for the intended player experience.
2. Design mechanics intended to produce target dynamics.
3. Review the resulting experience.
4. Redesign mechanics to improve alignment.

The study found MDA useful for mechanics design but insufficient for all the constraints of IP-based production. It therefore called for further work involving DPE, DDE, RMDA, and a proposed IP-MDA. [Webtoon-IP MDA study](https://www.koreascience.kr/article/JAKO202404861565963.page)

The 2026 analysis of *Split Fiction* applies MDA to a contemporary cooperative game, tracing forced two-player participation, asymmetric but equal-status roles, shared failure, low-cost retries, and chapter variation into cooperation dynamics and partnership-based experience. Its evidence consists of repeated play by one researcher and one fixed partner, supplemented by game text, development materials, and reviews. It is therefore a detailed single-case benchmark rather than a general validation of MDA. [MDA analysis of *Split Fiction*](https://doi.org/10.5392/jkca.2026.26.06.098)

### The main MDA extensions

#### RMDA: making the ontology more production-oriented

RMDA, or Redefining MDA, responds directly to the problem of ambiguous terms.

It defines a mechanic as the “doing responsibilities of Entities, with a purpose to invoke Dynamics.” The distinction separates an entity’s actions from the information it knows and excludes actions that merely support interaction without directly invoking a game dynamic. RMDA further divides mechanics into:

- Implied mechanics, such as running, jumping, or dying when those are expected by a genre.
- Core mechanics, such as shooting in a first-person shooter.
- Extra mechanics, such as camera shake or blur that differentiate a game and invoke particular dynamics.

RMDA defines dynamics as predictable runtime behaviors that emerge from mechanics and have a purpose to invoke aesthetics. It distinguishes simple dynamics, which emerge directly from mechanics, from complex dynamics, which emerge from other dynamics as well as mechanics. Aesthetics are reframed as desirable emotional responses that the player can invoke through interaction, emphasizing that the game offers conditions for emotion rather than directly controlling what a player feels.

Its practical process is reverse-oriented: define the main and secondary aesthetics, identify target dynamics, then specify and tune mechanics. The approach can reduce blind copying and make trade-offs explicit. Its limitation is evidential: RMDA is a conceptual ontology and framework proposal. The supplied research contains no controlled comparison showing that RMDA improves productivity, creativity, or player outcomes more than conventional MDA.

#### DDE: bringing the interface into the causal chain

DDE, Design–Dynamics–Experience, reframes the design-to-player relation by making player-facing experience more explicit. Walk, Görlich, and Barrett describe MDA as widely accepted but criticized for weaknesses. In DDE, the interface includes everything displayed, heard, or otherwise supplied as feedback because it translates abstract code into something the player can understand. [DDE framework chapter](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-319-53088-8_3)

The conceptual shift is significant. In MDA, aesthetics can be read as the intended emotional response; in DDE, experience and interface become more visible as design objects. A designer can therefore ask not only whether a rule produces a dynamic, but how feedback makes that dynamic legible, how the player interprets it, and how the resulting experience changes.

DDE is particularly useful for interface-heavy games, accessibility, onboarding, feedback design, and serious games. Its limitation is that the supplied evidence establishes a framework proposal, not empirical superiority over MDA.

#### DPE: foregrounding play and experience

DPE, Design–Play–Experience, emphasizes the player’s act of playing between design and experience. In educational-game contexts it adds learning, storytelling, gameplay, and user-experience levels to each of the three components. It can therefore expose relationships that MDA leaves implicit, such as how a learning objective is translated into a playable activity and then into an experienced outcome.

Its advantage is the explicit place for play and learning. Its weakness is translation: the RMDA paper notes that it is not always clear how DPE’s levels become concrete game elements. DPE is therefore useful for discussing the whole design-to-player pathway, but it requires additional specifications for mechanics, content, assessment, and implementation.

#### IP-MDA: adding transmedia-world constraints

IP-MDA retains MDA while inserting the source IP between the original world and the game system. The IP is analyzed through Mythos, Ethos, and Topos; those elements are translated into a Game IP organized around challenge, story, play, character, and premise; the resulting criteria guide mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics.

In the *White Day* case, Mythos included Korean folklore ghosts and a Yin–Yang and Five Elements system; Topos included Yeondu High School, the March 13–15, 2001 timeline, and White Day on March 14; Ethos included cultural norms, possession, revenge, and unresolved grudges. Seven developers independently reviewed a checklist across four iterations. The process produced a Yeokrin–5W1H system in which players uncover the reasons for ghosts’ deaths while avoiding emotional triggers and coping with time pressure. [IP-MDA study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723498.3723769)

IP-MDA’s strength is not that it creates a universal game-design ontology. Its strength is constraint management. It helps a team preserve cultural, narrative, and tonal properties while designing interactivity. Its limitation is that genre-specific balancing remained difficult, especially in a narrative-focused visual-novel format, and the study was a single case.

#### AI-enhanced MDA: adding generation and adaptation

An AI-enhanced MDA framework for educational games combines generative AI, adaptive learning algorithms, and procedural content generation with MDA and constructivist learning principles. It aims to support personalized, engaging, and scalable game-based learning. The source is explicit that this is theory synthesis and framework development, not an empirical comparison. Its effectiveness across diverse learning settings remains untested. [AI-enhanced MDA framework](https://doi.org/10.25304/rlt.v34.3746)

Its value is architectural: it asks where AI capabilities enter the MDA chain. Generative AI may alter mechanics or content; adaptive algorithms may alter dynamics; procedural generation may produce new spaces; educational models may define desired learning experiences. Its risk is that “AI-enhanced” can become a capability label without a validated account of whether adaptation improves learning, motivation, fairness, or comprehension.

## 3. Cutting-edge theories in contemporary game design

### Expectation Modulation: game feel can communicate through constraint

Conventional accounts of game feel often value responsiveness, fluid movement, and a strong sense of control. The 2025 theory of Expectation Modulation argues that emotionally expressive game feel may require deliberately violating those expectations.

The study used Constructivist Grounded Theory with interviews from 15 participants and analysis of 116 mechanics from *Journey*, *Celeste*, and *Freedom Bridge*. It proposed Expectation Modulation as a theory of how game feel can elicit emotional experience and identified nine design techniques, including Mechanical Subversion, Conscious Interactions, Re-contextualization, and Sensory Deprivation. [Expectation Modulation study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3723498.3723808)

The clearest example is *Journey*. In its penultimate blizzard scene, movement becomes progressively slower, heavier, and more laborious. The loss of responsiveness communicates exhaustion and hopelessness; the later flight and glide create catharsis through contrast. The mechanic does not empower the player in the conventional sense. It makes the player feel struggle through reduced capacity.

This theory addresses a real design phenomenon: control can be expressive rather than merely instrumental. A designer can use delay, friction, restricted movement, uncertainty, or sensory absence to represent grief, fatigue, vulnerability, or dependence.

Its evidence remains qualitative and theory-building. It does not establish that players universally prefer expressive constraint, nor does it resolve how much loss of control is meaningful before it becomes frustrating. The practical implication is to treat game feel as a semantic and emotional system. When evaluating responsiveness, designers should ask not only “Does the control feel good?” but “What does this responsiveness—or its absence—mean in the intended experience?”

### Experience-driven adaptation: from balancing performance to shaping emotion

The experience-driven adaptation loop treats player data as an input into an experience model and then changes content to influence the next player state. This is a control-system view of game design.

Its central claim is that a game can target more than success rate or challenge. It can target engagement, anxiety, calmness, immersion, stress, or therapeutic states. The evidence is strongest for the feasibility of sensing and adaptation in narrow prototypes and weakest for general claims about long-term welfare or universal flow.

#### Flow and dynamic difficulty

EDDA applies flow theory by treating challenge and player skill as variables that should remain within a workable channel. Excessive challenge may produce anxiety; insufficient challenge may produce boredom; both can contribute to quitting. EDDA adjusts difficulty using gameplay time within each challenge and monitors sleep, active, unit, and threshold phases alongside parameters at player, partner, opponent, and system levels. [EDDA study](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/15/10/5610)

The design advantage is operational clarity. A team can specify what is monitored, which threshold triggers an intervention, and which part of the game changes. The design danger is confusing a proxy with the experience itself. Time-on-task, accuracy, or physiological arousal can correlate with engagement or stress without uniquely identifying it.

The EDDA experiment illustrates that problem. Gameplay time and GEQ scores improved significantly, while overall fitness did not. A designer who measured only session length might declare success; a designer who measured challenge fitness might not. Both are observing different outcomes.

#### Physiological and facial-affect models

Physiological DDA uses signals such as eye tracking, electrodermal activity, heart rate, heart-rate variability, facial expression, voice level, and movement. A 2026 study trained a Random Forest on EDA and blood-volume-pulse data from 25 university students playing *Tetris*, *Sonic Racing*, and *Fall Guys*. It reported 86.01% accuracy, macro-AUC 0.98 across six discrete emotions, and sub-50-millisecond inference. The evaluation used a subject-independent train/test split, with EDA at 16 Hz, BVP at 64 Hz, and skin temperature at 1 Hz. [Neural Computing and Applications emotion study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00521-026-12307-5)

These numbers are useful for the engineering question “Can a classifier distinguish labels under this setup?” They do not establish that the system can infer a player’s true emotion in the wild. The labels came from frame-level facial analysis, while the classifier used EDA and BVP; movement, temperature, inter-person variation, weak signal-to-noise ratios, and class imbalance remain important confounds.

A 2026 emotion-driven game study combined facial-expression recognition with stage-completion time to switch among three difficulty levels and three genres. Among 26 university students, adaptive changes influenced physiological responses but did not change overall subjective satisfaction between groups. The result supports feasibility while weakening any claim that physiological influence automatically produces a better experience. [Saga and Sumi](https://www.atlantis-press.com/proceedings/wctp-25/126023787)

#### Closed-loop emotion regulation

The VEE-Loop theory—Virtual Emotion, Elicitation and Recognition Loop—extends the adaptation idea into a closed loop: the system recognizes an affective state, changes the virtual environment, and uses the changed environment to elicit or regulate subsequent emotion. It applies to entertainment, training, education, product design, manufacturing, and therapy. [VEE-Loop](https://www.sciexplor.com/ec/articles/ec.2026.0019)

The theory identifies advantages of VR for contextual grounding, embodied interaction, multimodal synchronization, repeatability, and personalized calibration. It also identifies the central difficulties: emotions transition continuously, ground truth is ambiguous, multimodal data are noisy, motion artifacts interfere with sensing, and real-time computation is expensive. Motion, gaze, and physiological data can be highly identifying, requiring robust consent, governance, and secure storage.

VEE-Loop is therefore best understood as a design architecture and research agenda, not a validated therapeutic method. Its strongest practical contribution is forcing teams to specify the entire loop: what state is recognized, how uncertainty is represented, what adaptation occurs, what outcome is desired, and how harm is detected.

### ExpREx: designing toward an experience specification

ExpREx, or Experience Regular Expressions, treats emotional experience goals as computable specifications for procedural level generation. Fernandes, Lopes, and Prada combine evolutionary algorithms, data-driven persona agents, predictive emotional models, and a parameterized level generator. They evolved levels toward target experiences for different player subsets and evaluated congruence using continuous player annotations.

In a study of 101 participants, 93.73% of the targeted ExpREx goals were also reported by study subjects. [Generating Game Levels by Defining Player Experiences](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AIIDE/article/view/31878)

The theory addresses a major limitation of conventional PCG. Random or rule-based generation can produce valid levels without producing the intended experience. ExpREx places experience targets before or alongside content generation.

The result is promising but bounded. The supplied abstract does not specify a control condition, the number of targeted goals, the game genre, the model-training data, or the number of player subsets. The percentage therefore indicates target-response congruence within the study, not superiority over human-authored levels or general reliability across games.

The practical implication is to separate content validity from experience validity. A generated level should be tested not only for reachability, balance, and technical correctness but also for whether players report the intended tension, relief, curiosity, or mastery.

### Procedural rhetoric and Values at Play: games as arguments and value systems

Procedural rhetoric treats rules and mechanics as a way of persuading or communicating ideas. Its concern is not merely whether a game produces challenge or fellowship, but what the player learns, normalizes, questions, or enacts through the system. A related CTV cycle—Conceptualization, Translation, Verification—makes the design process explicit.

The *Poder Violeta 2* case in Bogotá demonstrates the difference. The game addresses sexual harassment on public transportation and requires players to evade harassers, making vulnerability and resistance playable rather than merely narrating them. A participatory process involved 30 university students from Bogotá, six workshops, collective drawing, discussion, consensus, and five protagonist versions. The intended audience was especially young men aged 15–29. [Poder Violeta 2](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sociology/articles/10.3389/fsoc.2025.1596630/full)

The earlier version had represented victims passively and left the protagonist mechanically disadvantaged. Feminist collectives identified those problems during verification. The later design added multiple playable characters and power-ups to increase agency and representation. The authors explicitly do not claim that the game alone directly changes behavior or reduces harassment.

Values at Play provides a complementary workflow: discover values, identify them, translate them into design, and verify their presence and effects. The Roblox harmful-design study recommends value guidance before creator ideation, reflection during ideation, and iterative validation during implementation, while acknowledging uncertainty about whether child creators can assimilate the guidance.

The limitation is shared by many values-sensitive approaches: identifying a value in a design does not prove that players adopt it. A game can represent agency while making the player powerless, criticize exploitation while rewarding it, or depict inclusion while excluding people from authorship. Verification must therefore examine mechanics, dynamics, representation, player interpretation, and consequences.

### Affective User-Centred Design

Affective User-Centred Design extends user-centred practice by treating emotional response as a design requirement. A 2026 study reports statistically significant relationships between affective design elements and deep engagement in indie games and proposes a rank-ordered AUCD framework to help developers prioritize features. The supplied record does not provide the underlying dataset or effect sizes, and it does not present an MDA analysis or test an MDA extension. [AUCD study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10209-025-01291-7)

The practical value of AUCD lies in making affective intent explicit during research and evaluation. It is especially useful when the design goal is not a single emotion but a sustained relationship among emotional response, gameplay, interface, and player identity. Its unresolved problem is measurement: a rank order derived from survey relationships may not transfer across genres, cultures, player expertise, or long-term play.

### Mixed-initiative co-creative AI

Mixed-initiative systems divide creative control between human and AI. The central theoretical issue is not whether the model can generate a level or asset, but who decides the design direction, when the AI acts, how its initiative is communicated, and whether the designer can understand and revise its proposals.

A 2025 systematic review of human–AI co-creativity retained 62 papers from an initial pool of 2,668 English-language papers published from 2015 to 2023. It found that high user control was associated with satisfaction, trust, and ownership, while proactive AI could deepen collaboration when adaptive and context-sensitive. It also identified gaps in early creative phases such as problem clarification and in user adaptation to AI tools. [Human–AI co-creativity review](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.21333)

The Evolutionary Dungeon Designer study provides counterevidence to a simple “more AI initiative is better” assumption. Three levels of AI agency produced frustration and relationship strains for human designers. A system that makes surprising changes may produce novelty, but it can also violate the designer’s mental model and create costly repair work. [Evolutionary Dungeon Designer study](https://doi.org/10.1609/aiide.v18i1.21957)

A useful theory of co-creative design must therefore model initiative, reversibility, explanation, ownership, and repair. The designer needs to know not only what the system changed, but why, what constraints it used, and how to preserve or reject the change.

### Self-determination, retention, and player welfare

Self-Determination Theory explains motivation through autonomy, competence, and relatedness. In contemporary live-service design, those needs interact with retention systems, rewards, social comparison, and monetization.

Park and Yap used 2.5 years of netnography and 11,246 posts from one mobile-game community to identify mechanisms through which game design affects psychological needs. They argue that features that stimulate flow and immersion can support revenue while also creating tension with consumer welfare. [Park and Yap](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144929X.2025.2492699)

A 2026 thesis combined MDA, AARRR—Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Revenue, Referral—and SDT to analyze *Fortnite*, *Genshin Impact*, and *Valorant*, alongside an open-ended survey of 38 respondents. It describes retention-oriented systems that sustain commercial engagement without necessarily sustaining satisfaction, with FOMO maintaining participation even when players describe their experience negatively. Perceived exchange value moderated distress: players were more accepting when rewards seemed commensurate with demands and more distressed when the system produced obligation or disruption. [Live-service MDA, AARRR, and SDT analysis](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2073544/FULLTEXT01.pdf)

This is a case-based analysis, not a population estimate. Its importance lies in showing that MDA can analyze commercial mechanics as mechanics. XP requirements, reward tracks, limited-time content, and progression gates are mechanics; repeated login, optimization, and spending are dynamics; satisfaction, urgency, pressure, or compulsion are possible aesthetics.

## 4. Emerging technologies and production practices

### Official tools versus measured design outcomes

Official product documentation is valuable for establishing what a tool can do. It is not evidence that the tool improves player experience, originality, productivity, or design quality. The difference is especially important because product announcements often describe intended workflows and future roadmaps.

| Tool or system | Documented capability | Evidence type | What remains unavailable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unity Muse | Editor-integrated Chat, animation generation and editing, behavior-tree assistance, asset and code support | Official Unity announcement | Independent productivity, quality, originality, and player-outcome measures |
| Unreal PCG | Node-based procedural generation for assets, biomes, and worlds with real-time editor updates | Official Epic documentation | Controlled evidence of production savings or player benefit |
| Roblox Cube | Text-to-3D mesh generation in Studio and Lua API; future roadmap toward functional “4D” creation | Official Roblox announcement | Independent evaluation of generated quality, originality, and runtime robustness |
| Roblox Build | Mobile-first text-to-game workflow, playtesting, analytics, and experiment agents; public alpha in New Zealand from July 28, 2026 | Official Roblox announcement | Outcomes beyond rollout and stated product aims |
| AutoUE | Multi-agent Unreal workflow for retrieval, scene generation, code synthesis, and automated playtesting | 2026 scholarly prototype | Broad validation of quality, productivity, maintainability, or player experience |

### Unity Muse and mixed-initiative editor work

Unity’s official announcement says all five Muse capabilities became available directly in the Unity Editor. Muse Chat is project-aware; Muse Animate generates and edits humanoid animation clips; Muse Behavior converts natural-language logic into human-readable nodes and branches, with a blackboard for reusable variables and custom actions. The described design impact is practical: repeated actions can be duplicated, and complex interactions can be prototyped more quickly. [Unity Muse capabilities](https://unity.com/blog/engine-platform/unity-muse-ai-capabilities-in-editor-plus-new-updates)

The evidence does not establish how much time teams save after correction, review, debugging, integration, and art direction. A behavior tree that is easy to generate can still be wrong in edge cases, conflict with narrative pacing, or produce uninteresting dynamics. The appropriate production pattern is therefore proposal, inspection, constrained implementation, playtest, and revision.

Microsoft Research’s Muse announcement describes WHAM as a generative AI model that can generate game visuals, controller actions, or both. It presents the model as a support for human creativity and gameplay ideation. The supplied evidence establishes a model capability and creative objective, not a player-outcome study. [Microsoft Research on Muse and WHAM](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/video/introducing-muse-our-first-generative-ai-model-designed-for-gameplay-ideation/)

### Unreal PCG and constraint-based generation

Epic describes Unreal Engine’s Procedural Content Generation Framework as a toolset for technical artists, designers, and programmers, ranging from asset utilities such as buildings and biome generation to entire worlds. A PCG graph passes spatial data through nodes that generate, filter, and modify points; outputs can spawn assets and update in real time in the editor. [Unreal PCG documentation](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/procedural-content-generation-overview?lang=en-US)

The forest example sets density to 0.15 points per square meter, scales instances from 0.5 to 1.2, randomizes rotation from 0 to 360 degrees, and spawns trees. These values show how a designer specifies variation and density; they do not show whether the resulting forest is more interesting, faster to author, or more performant than a hand-authored one.

This distinction captures the value of PCG. It moves repetition and variation into an explicit parameter space, allowing designers to tune distributions rather than place every object. It also creates a new design responsibility: the generator must preserve navigability, sightlines, pacing, affordances, and aesthetic coherence. A visually plausible output can still produce blocked routes, unfair encounters, or meaningless space.

A 2026 Roblox study makes constraint validation explicit. Its Luau system combines random placement with boundary checks, Euclidean-distance overlap checks, restricted-zone checks, and cross-type relations among enemies, treasure chests, and traps. In ten sessions on a 1,000-by-1,000-stud map containing 340 enemies, 10 chests, and 50 traps, the system reported no constraint violations and maintained playability, with average spawning time of 336.62 milliseconds per session. The scope was one map size, one object configuration, and ten sessions, so it establishes functional feasibility rather than broad quality. [Rule-Based Random Generation in Roblox](https://doi.org/10.59934/jaiea.v5i3.2307)

### Roblox Cube and Build

Roblox announced Cube 3D in March 2025 as an open-source 3D foundation model with a beta mesh-generation API in Roblox Studio and an in-experience Lua API. The model tokenizes 3D shapes and uses an autoregressive transformer to predict the next shape token. At launch, the documented capability was text-to-object generation; image inputs, full-scene generation, scene understanding, and contextual edits were described as future directions. [Roblox Cube](https://about.roblox.com/newsroom/2025/03/introducing-roblox-cube)

Roblox’s concept of “4D creation” treats interaction among objects, environments, and people as the fourth dimension. This is an important design ambition because a static mesh is not yet a game object. A creator needs collision, affordances, state, animation, scripting, social meaning, and performance constraints. The announcement is a roadmap, however, not evidence that generated scenes reliably provide those properties.

On July 28, 2026, Roblox announced public alpha access for selected Build features, including publishing, in New Zealand for age-checked users aged 9 and older. Published games passing safety checks were described as globally available to age-checked users aged 16 and older. The announcement frames Build as a mobile-first text-to-game starting point and describes playtesting, analytics, and experiment agents across Build and Studio, in the context of 132 million daily active users. It remains a limited public alpha, and the final feature set may change. [Roblox Build announcement](https://about.roblox.com/newsroom/2026/07/build-without-limits-on-roblox)

For design, text-to-game tools alter the entry point from implementation to intention. That can make experimentation accessible to more people, but it also raises the importance of constraint literacy. A creator who can describe a game but cannot inspect generated logic may have less control than a conventional creator using a smaller but legible toolset.

### AutoUE and end-to-end generation

AutoUE, described in a 2026 Findings of ACL paper, is a multi-agent system for generating complete Unreal Engine games. It coordinates model retrieval, scene generation, gameplay and interaction-code synthesis, and automated game testing. The system uses an embedding database containing more than 858,000 3D models and a dataset of 20 game-generation tasks. [AutoUE](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.111.pdf)

The workflow separates a natural-language prompt into a scene description and a gameplay description. The scene description covers context and key objects; the gameplay description covers mechanics and player interactions. This split responds to a common design failure: prompts often interleave what should exist with what should happen, confusing downstream generation.

AutoUE also retrieves engine documentation through retrieval-augmented generation, adds common design patterns and engine constraints during code generation, and uses Model Context Protocol runtime commands for automated playtesting. The authors report higher-quality 3D scenes than existing approaches, but also emphasize that engine-integrated 3D generation remains non-trivial because spatial layouts, gameplay behavior, and multiple subsystems must coordinate.

This is a meaningful production practice: generated code should be checked in the runtime environment, not merely inspected as text. Static validation can confirm syntax or object existence; playtesting is needed to reveal unreachable goals, broken interaction sequences, timing problems, and dynamics that only appear after several actions.

### What human-in-the-loop evidence shows

The strongest counterweight to autonomous-generation claims comes from direct prototype studies.

*The Ink Splotch Effect* created nine minimalist Unity games across three genres—arcade space shooter, platformer, and turn-based roguelike—with baseline, human-designed, and ChatGPT-suggested variants. A blind user study assessed quality, game feel, innovation, and preference. The study provides a concrete comparison, but the graphics were minimalist and the supplied record does not state the sample size. [The Ink Splotch Effect](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.02454)

The human designer used iterative playtesting to improve communication of damage through screen effects, sound, particles, and screen shake. In the ChatGPT-guided space shooter, a teleport ability placed the player on an enemy or in the wrong position; a later bug made the player disappear. ChatGPT could not resolve the problem after repeated attempts, and the designers repaired the z-axis error manually. In the roguelike, suggested room generation and enemy-patrol features remained unimplemented because of bugs and contextual misunderstandings.

A practice-led 3D-asset comparison found that an AI-assisted reconstruction of a stylized fantasy tavern took 238 minutes, compared with 716.06 minutes for a human-authored scene. Yet the AI pipeline produced dense triangulated geometry, fragmented UV maps, inconsistent prompt adherence, material-editing constraints, clipping, and texture loss during attempted decimation. The study supports AI for ideation, rough-prop exploration, and early prototyping, while retaining artists and technical artists for retopology, UVs, materials, art direction, optimization, and engine validation. [Prompted Props, Human Pipelines](https://www.ijhrsss.com/articles/380)

The design conclusion is not “AI is fast” or “AI is unreliable.” It is that first-pass speed and finished-production cost are different variables. A useful production measure should include prompting, selection, correction, integration, debugging, optimization, legal review, and playtesting.

### LLMs in player modeling and game architecture

A 2025 Unity proof of concept integrated an LLM into player modeling. It read score, remaining lives, and time left every two seconds, compared behavior with four Bartle profiles, and used a coin-collection game with five lives as its testbed. Across 50 input-output pairs, G-Eval produced a mean correctness score of 4.044 out of 5, with 75% scoring at least 4; 750 evaluations were performed across Gemini 2.0 Flash, Meta LLaMA 3, and GPT-4o. The test used simulated random behavior rather than observed human play, so output correctness is not evidence of improved player experience. [LLM player modeling study](https://sol.sbc.org.br/index.php/sbgames/article/download/37373/37155/)

The study identifies cold start and data volume as unresolved problems. Little is known about a player at the beginning of a game, while accurate player models often require large volumes of multimodal data. LLM-based evaluation may also be biased toward outputs from similar models.

A 2026 controlled prototype comparing Unity object-oriented architecture with data-oriented design through ECS found ECS outperformed OOP under high-frequency LLM query loads. This result points to an architectural trade-off: generative content changes not only authoring but also runtime data flow. [Unity OOP and ECS comparison](https://experts.nau.edu/en/publications/evaluating-the-effect-of-generative-ai-content-in-common-game-dev/)

A separate 2026 controlled mixed-methods experiment with 31 participants compared Unreal Blueprints and Unity Visual Scripting using correctness, efficiency, a method-evaluation model, and focus groups. The reported result favored Blueprints across all metrics, attributing the advantage to a tailored abstraction layer, model-based debugging, and bidirectional Blueprint–C++ integration. The supplied conference page is marked tentative, so the result should be treated as preliminary. [Blueprints and Unity Visual Scripting study](https://conf.researchr.org/details/models-2026/models-2026-research-papers/22/The-Software-Modeling-Paradox-in-Videogames-An-Empirical-Evaluation-of-Unreal-Bluepr)

### Haptics, accessibility, and embodied production

The technical challenge in haptic design is authoring meaningful correspondence. A haptic event may represent collision, weight, damage, bodily exertion, emotional shock, or a UI state. The same vibration pattern can therefore have different meanings depending on timing and context.

The 2025 wearable haptic-device study for children with visual impairments recommends two-player adaptation for social interaction, multiple difficulty levels, varied haptic feedback, and customizable audio. It uses qualitative and quantitative testing but reports no numerical effect sizes. [Wearable haptic device study](https://doi.org/10.54963/dtra.v4i2.1226)

This is consistent with the broader accessibility principle documented in the Xbox guidelines: accessibility is not a single toggle. It is a set of mechanics, representations, feedback channels, timing rules, and social assumptions that need to be tested with the people affected.

## 5. Practical applications and named game-design cases

### Case 1: *Split Fiction* and mandatory cooperation

The 2026 MDA study of Hazelight’s *Split Fiction* is a useful contemporary example because it demonstrates how a high-level aesthetic can become a structural requirement.

| MDA element | *Split Fiction* design | Expected or observed result |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanics | Two-player simultaneous participation, equal-status asymmetric roles, shared progression, joint failure, low-cost retries | Solo completion is excluded; both players are needed |
| Dynamics | Division of labor, timing alignment, cooperation vocabulary, strategy adjustment after failure | Players coordinate, communicate, and revise plans together |
| Aesthetics | Shared achievement, challenge experienced as partnership, companionship | Cooperation feels like the substance of play rather than an optional bonus |
| Implementation | Interdependent chapter-specific gimmicks and role variation | The game can vary cooperation without abandoning its central premise |
| Evidence limit | Repeated play by one researcher and one fixed partner, plus text, reviews, and development materials | Strong single-case interpretation; no population-level generalization |

The important mechanism is not merely that two players are present. It is that the mechanics make their goals and capacities interdependent. Shared failure prevents one player from treating the other as disposable; low-cost retries reduce the social cost of experimentation; equal-status asymmetry avoids making one participant a permanent assistant.

The study reports functional division of labor, timing alignment, a shared cooperative vocabulary, strategic adjustment across failure–retry cycles, and emotional buffering. Replay is interpreted as a desire to share the journey with a new partner or exchange roles rather than primarily to explore branching content.

For designers, the evaluation criteria are concrete:

- Can each player explain what the other contributes?
- Are roles asymmetric without becoming unequal in status?
- Does failure create information and conversation rather than blame?
- Is the cost of retrying low enough to encourage experimentation?
- Does chapter variation change the form of cooperation rather than merely reskin it?

The case does not show that mandatory cooperation is generally superior to optional cooperation. It shows how a design goal can be made structurally legible through MDA.

### Case 2: Adaptive difficulty and stress-sensitive play

*Code: Terror* shows how a stress-adaptive design can reverse familiar difficulty logic. Its Relax-to-Win strategy rewards calmness: lower stress increases the chance of success, while rising stress makes the game more difficult. The system combines smartwatch heart rate, voice level, and heart-rate variability with in-game behavior. In the 40-participant study, dynamic difficulty produced higher motivation and engagement-related scores and lower heart-rate ranges. [Code: Terror study](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/19/3870)

The intended dynamic is distinctive. A conventional horror game may intensify fear to create engagement. Relax-to-Win instead makes emotional regulation part of the challenge. The design goal is not simply “scare the player,” but “make calmness mechanically consequential.”

That approach introduces risks:

- If stress measurement is noisy, the difficulty may change for the wrong reason.
- If stress rises because the game is exciting rather than harmful, the intervention may suppress the intended aesthetic.
- If difficulty increases while a player is already overwhelmed, the system may amplify frustration.
- If the player cannot understand why the game changed, the system may feel unfair.

The Caroline and VR counterexamples are therefore essential. Biofeedback improved intrinsic motivation in one case but not other experience dimensions; damage-based adaptation in another increased frustration. A stress-sensitive mechanic requires parameter testing, transparency decisions, and welfare boundaries.

The 2025 physiological-DDA study offers another implementation pattern. Rather than infer an abstract emotion, it predicts challenge and engagement from physiological responses and uses those predictions to select difficulty. Its small N=10 model-development and N=12 evaluation samples support a promising prototype, not a general player model.

### Case 3: *Journey* and expressive loss of control

*Journey* demonstrates Expectation Modulation more clearly than a generic discussion of game feel. The player begins with movement that communicates agency and exploration. In the blizzard, movement slows and becomes heavy. The mechanic produces a dynamic of effort without mastery, supporting an aesthetic of struggle. When movement becomes powerful again, the contrast produces release.

The design decision is not “make controls worse.” It is “make reduced capability legible as an emotional event.” To apply this responsibly, a team should establish:

- What expectation is being modulated?
- What emotion should the modulation support?
- How long can the constraint last before it becomes irritation?
- What audiovisual or narrative cues explain the change?
- What later mechanic restores or transforms the lost capability?

This model is especially relevant to games about fatigue, grief, vulnerability, dependence, or transformation. It also shows why game feel cannot be reduced to responsiveness as a universal good.

### Case 4: Live-service systems in *Fortnite*, *Genshin Impact*, and *Valorant*

MDA can analyze live-service systems without endorsing them. In the 2026 thesis, mechanics include XP requirements, progression structures, reward tracks, limited-time events, and monetization gates. Dynamics include increased login frequency, challenge optimization, extended sessions, and spending decisions. Aesthetics include progression satisfaction, urgency, pressure, obligation, and frustration. [Live-service case analysis](https://uu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2073544/FULLTEXT01.pdf)

AARRR adds a commercial lifecycle: acquisition, activation, retention, revenue, and referral. SDT adds autonomy, competence, and relatedness. The three frameworks answer different questions:

- MDA: What system rules produce which patterns of play and experience?
- AARRR: Where does the player enter, remain, spend, and recruit others?
- SDT: Which psychological needs are supported or undermined?

The thesis’s 38-person open-ended survey and three game cases suggest that FOMO can maintain engagement even when satisfaction falls. This is a design distinction with practical consequences. Retention is not equivalent to enjoyment, and a successful acquisition or revenue mechanic may produce pressure rather than a healthy experience.

The analytical pay-to-win model by Deng and colleagues provides a counterpoint. It defines pay-to-win as purchasing superior equipment that increases winning odds in player-versus-player games. In its monopolistic-developer model with version-specific network effects, tournament design can make freemium optimal and can produce a Pareto improvement for the developer and all players. That conclusion is model-based and depends on its assumptions; it is not a field study showing that commercial pay-to-win systems improve player welfare. [Pay-to-win analytical model](https://doi.org/10.1287/isre.2023.0258)

Pokémon TCG Live provides a useful counterexample to the assumption that digital trading-card games require direct monetization. A 2024 case study describes it as having no direct monetization while examining how its close relationship with the printed Pokémon TCG shapes the online client. [Pokémon TCG Live case study](https://doi.org/10.34135/actaludologica.2024-7-1.74-85)

For practice, the question is not whether monetization exists but which dynamic it produces. Does it support collection, expression, and fellowship? Does it create urgency, exclusion, obligation, or unequal competition? Does the value exchange remain legible?

### Case 5: *Poder Violeta 2* and critical design

*Poder Violeta 2* demonstrates the difference between communicating a social message through narrative and embedding it in mechanics. Players evade harassers, so vulnerability and resistance are enacted. The design uses procedural rhetoric: the rules communicate a claim about lived experience.

The earlier version’s problems show why participatory verification matters. Feminist collectives identified passive victim representation and a mechanic that always left the protagonist at a disadvantage. The project’s second phase expanded participation, introduced multiple protagonists, and added power-ups to increase agency and representation.

The practical evaluation criteria are not only “Does the game discuss harassment?” but:

- Who has agency?
- What behavior is rewarded?
- Is vulnerability represented as a fixed identity or a social condition?
- Can players understand the system’s critique through action?
- Did people represented by the design participate in its interpretation?
- What evidence would count as learning or reflection?
- What claims should the game explicitly avoid making?

The authors’ refusal to claim direct behavior change is a methodological strength. A critical game can create reflection without directly changing conduct, and a designer should not confuse a compelling message with a measured social effect.

### Case 6: GameIN and shared play

GameIN’s co-design process with neurodivergent adults treats inclusion as contact with participants’ everyday contexts and continuous iteration. Its primary objective is playing together regardless of skills and specificities, rather than creating a separate therapeutic product.

This changes the MDA analysis. Accessibility is not simply an aesthetic outcome added after mechanics are complete. It shapes mechanics from the beginning:

- A shared action may need multiple input timings.
- A challenge may need adjustable sensory intensity.
- A social role may need to support observation, participation, or assistance.
- The feedback system may need parallel visual, audio, textual, and haptic channels.
- The group dynamic must tolerate different speeds and attention patterns.

The source provides no standardized comparative measure, so the result is best treated as participatory design evidence and a practical case, not a causal estimate.

### Case 7: Roblox’s live UGC dynamics

Naavik’s industry report describes Roblox’s 2025 “Admin Abuse War” involving *Grow A Garden* and *Steal A Brainrot*. Administrators entered live games, altered statistics, and gave players unusually large amounts of content, creating unscripted and highly shareable events. *Grow A Garden* reportedly reached 21.3 million concurrent users in June 2025; *Steal A Brainrot* later reached 25.4 million in October. Both audiences subsequently declined, illustrating the difference between viral acceleration and durable retention. [Naavik’s UGC report](https://naavik.co/deep-dives/the-state-of-ugc-games-2026/)

The MDA reading is straightforward:

- Mechanics: administrator powers, mutable statistics, gifting, timed events, collection systems, and social visibility.
- Dynamics: anticipation, crowd migration, rivalry, speculation, sharing, and participation in a live spectacle.
- Aesthetics: surprise, belonging, status, urgency, and communal excitement.

The design lesson is that live operations can become a performance layer. The administrator is not merely balancing numbers; they are producing a social event that players can witness, record, and circulate.

The caveat is equally important. The figures come from an industry report, and viral concurrency is not the same as satisfaction, accessibility, or healthy community norms. If live events privilege constant attention, randomized gifts, or social pressure, they may create welfare costs that raw engagement conceals.

### Case 8: AI-assisted prototyping

*The Ink Splotch Effect* and the stylized tavern asset study provide a practical workflow:

1. Use AI to produce options or a rough implementation.
2. Inspect the output against the intended mechanic and aesthetic.
3. Test it in the engine.
4. Identify bugs, context failures, or technical debt.
5. Repair manually or regenerate under tighter constraints.
6. Playtest the repaired version.
7. Measure the result against a human-authored baseline where possible.

This workflow is compatible with MDA. A generated asset or script is not evaluated only for existence. It is evaluated for the dynamics it enables and the aesthetics it supports. A teleport script that technically executes but places the player inside an enemy has failed at the dynamics layer; a generated environment that looks attractive but blocks navigation has failed at the mechanics-to-dynamics relationship.

### Case 9: IP-MDA and *White Day*

The *White Day* case is useful for teams adapting a franchise because it shows how mechanics can preserve identity without copying surface elements. The team did not simply reproduce ghosts, school corridors, or visual motifs. It translated Mythos, Ethos, and Topos into a Game IP, then tested whether mechanics expressed the intended cultural and dramatic properties.

The four iterations show why IP design cannot be reduced to an asset checklist. The team moved from eliminating ghosts, to understanding their deaths, to distinguishing truth from falsehood, and finally to uncovering truth while avoiding Yeokrin triggers under time pressure. Each iteration changed the dynamic and the emotional meaning of the interaction.

The practical result was a verification checklist that could be used across director, design, UI, writing, programming, and art roles. Its limitation is that genre-specific requirements remained difficult, especially where a visual novel’s narrative choices conflicted with action-oriented systems.

## 6. Comparing MDA with newer design approaches

No supplied source reports a direct controlled comparison of MDA with DDE, DPE, RMDA, or IP-MDA. The comparison below therefore concerns what each framework makes visible and what design problem it is equipped to address, not verified superiority.

### Framework comparison

| Approach | Primary causal path | Main design object | Best use case | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MDA | Mechanics → dynamics → aesthetics | Rules, runtime behavior, intended experience | Shared vocabulary, system tuning, game analysis | Loose ontology; weak coverage of interface, context, values, and production workflow |
| RMDA | Aesthetic objectives → target dynamics → categorized mechanics | Explicit mechanics and predictable dynamics | Production communication and intentional tuning | Conceptual proposal without head-to-head empirical validation |
| DDE | Design → dynamics → experience, with interface as translation layer | Feedback, interface, and player-facing experience | UX, feedback, onboarding, serious games | Limited evidence of adoption or superior outcomes |
| DPE | Design → play → experience, with learning/story/gameplay/UX levels | The act of play and outcome formation | Educational and experience-centered design | Translation from levels to concrete mechanics can remain unclear |
| IP-MDA | Source IP → Game IP → mechanics/dynamics/aesthetics | Transmedia world, dramatic elements, and interactive expression | Franchise and transmedia adaptation | Case-based; genre-specific balancing remains difficult |
| Procedural rhetoric and CTV | Values or argument → rules and procedures → interpretation and verification | What systems communicate or normalize | Critical games, social change, political design | Intent and representation do not prove persuasion or behavior change |
| Adaptive-experience loop | Sensed data → player model → content intervention → new data | Runtime adaptation and player state | Personalized challenge, therapy, immersive systems | Sensing noise, opacity, privacy, and small-sample validation |
| Mixed-initiative AI | Human intention ↔ AI proposal ↔ human revision | Allocation of initiative and authorship | Ideation, prototyping, content generation | Frustration, ownership loss, bugs, context failure, and unclear responsibility |

### MDA, RMDA, DDE, and DPE: what changes in the causal lens?

MDA is primarily a system-to-experience model. It begins with what the designer builds and asks what play pattern and emotional response result.

RMDA preserves the same basic relationship but makes the design sequence more explicit. It distinguishes implied, core, and extra mechanics and limits “dynamics” to behaviors a team can reasonably identify during an iteration. Its purpose is operational clarity.

DDE shifts attention toward design and interface. This matters because a mechanic cannot produce a meaningful player experience if the player cannot perceive its state, understand its affordance, or interpret its feedback. DDE is therefore stronger when the design problem is translation from code to player understanding.

DPE inserts play as a central process. This is useful when the outcome depends on how the player interprets, learns, or performs the design rather than on the system alone. Educational games particularly benefit from distinguishing a designed learning objective from what players actually do and experience.
